maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals whether or not he has taken into consideration _ the report of the committee which investigated some matters in dispute between the management of the Intercolonial Railway and the freight clerks at Halifax and St. John. I observe some rather important statements in the report of the

committee which have, no doubt, been dTawn to the minister's attention and which perhaps he has considered. I quote from the report as brought down in a return to this House, page 4:-
Accordingly, and after full discussion, the following matters were agreed upon by all parties in the form as under:
Your committee are of opinion that it would make for greater harmony and better efficiency if a system of classification of clerks were introduced. Not only would the above results accrue, but there would then be an available scheme for promotion, which at the present time seems to be lacking, and which omission breeds discontent owing to the uncertainty of upward progress for efficient clerks who have by length of service and attention to the duties of their office earned the right to consideration in this regard. Just what system of classification should be introduced must neessarily be evolved by the offi-ials of the railway who are more intimately familiar with the details of the business of the Intercolonial than your committee can possibly be. The men involved must necessarily accept the classification determined upon, subject, of course, to the right which they possess of bringing to the attention of their superiors in office any improvement in such classification which to them may seem desirable in the best interests of the service.
Further on, at page 5, dealing with promotion, the report says:
Your committee are further strongly of the opinion that, outside of the rare cases that arise where an exceptionally able outsider is brought into the service to fill some particular position requiring special knowledge and training, the principle of promotion of those already in the service should obtain, having due regard, of course, to efficiency and the requirements of the service.
And further on, at page 7:
The committee further considered the question involved and now submit the following additional recommendations:	The committee
after its investigation, is of opinion that, in the matter of wages, the system that obtains of appointing from time to time, new men at higher pay over the heads of men long in the service and probably more capable of doing the work, is injurious to the service and unjust to the men. The remedy for this lies in reorganization, and the abolition of the existing system of appointment influenced by political patronage, which from the point of efficient working we find ample evidence to condemn as applied to the Intercolonial Railway.
I do not bring this up to-day for the purpose of making any animadversions upon or indulging in any criticism of the department, but merely for the purpose of inquiring whether the attention of the minister has been fully directed to this report, whether he has the recommendations under consideration, as I have no doubt he has, whether he has arrived. at

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: any conclusion as to what can be done and, if he is not able to give us his conclusions to-day, whether or not we may expect to hear them at a reasonably early date.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I may not be orthodox, but I cannot agree with any suggestion that makes length of service an absolute qualification for promotion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Not the only one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: To my mind ability to perform the duties is the supreme test. That, coupled with length of service ought to bring about the promotion of the individual. This report of the board was brought to my attention the other day by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) on going into Committee of Supply, I think, and if I remember correctly my reply was that action had not been taken as yet, one of the reasons being that the report implies the dismissal of several employees. In order to ascertain just how that report should be carried out, without doing injustice to an employee, I am having an investigation made into the whole situation as to length of service, ability and all that kind of necessary information with regard to each clerk in so far as I can get it. When that is done I intend to proceed along the lines of the report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
With regard to the report just referred to, I would like to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to the fact, that the other day, in speaking about the Intercolonial Railway, he stated that so far from the Intercolonial being overmanned it was not manned to the same extent as some other railways in Canada. If that is the case it would appear that the clerks in the employ of the Intercolonial Railway at Halifax and St. John are not too numerous and consequently this report can hardly be correct in that respect. Either the minister is wrong or the report is wrong, so that it would appear to me that the course of the minister is absolutely clear; that is he has to put those men in these two cities, working for the Intercolonial Railway, on a proper basis as regards pay, and I think, judging from the report that has been read, it was quite allowed by the reporters that the men there are not paid sufficiently. The statement was also made that the road was overmanned, that there were more than sufficient to do the work and that the salaries paid in excess of the requirements should be divided amongst those who are retained. But, taking into consideration the statement that the minister himself made the other day with regard to the manning of the Intercolonial Railway that it was not manned to
the same extent as some other railways were, I would think that the case was rather plain for the granting of an increase in pay to the clerks at the railway 'terminal at Halifax and St. John.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
I would like to have had an opportunity of seeing this report but it has just come to my hand at this moment, I do not understand that this board of conciliation were appointed to deal with the question as to whether there were too many men on the Intercolonial Railway or whether there were not enough. I understand that this board were commissioned to ascertain whether the men on the Intercolonial Railway were properly paid or not. Therefore, I do not see what right they had to come and tell the Minister of Railways and Canals that his department was overmanned. I believe they overstepped the bounds in doing that, particularly as we had the Minister of Railways the other day stating distinctly that the Intercolonial was not manned to the extent of any other railway in the Dominion of Canada, a statement which was corroborated by statistics. Therefore, I think that settles the question and I do not think that this commision will be in a position to make a report that would be as definite as the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals himself. I think we can set aside altogether the question as to whether the Intercolonial Railway at St. John and Halifax is overmanned but, upon the question as to whether the men were in receipt of sufficient pay or not, the board reported distinctly that the men were not paid enough and recommended an increase to them. I am not going to deal with the matter of qualification and other questions touched upon in the report as I suppose we will have an opportunity of taking those questions up on some future occasion, but I really do think that whatever may be done in connection with this report the clerks who were willing to come under the conciliation clause of the Act known as the Lemieux Act and who have been willing to allow that board to be appointed, feeling that they would get fair play are entitled to be fairly dealt with in that respect. Whatever may be done with regard to the manning of the railway, if the minister should find upon investigation that such has occurred, I really think he should take this matter up himself because it is not a matter for the board to deal with. I am convinced from the statistics quoted here the other day, from the very exhaustive discussion that we had and from the elaborate references to the whole matter of railways in the Dominion of Canada that the intercolonial is not overmanned as compared with other railways. The clerks have made an appeal, in fact, I think they went out on strike almost, or threatened to go out,
they have accepted this board and they should have that which is due to them by the authority and report of the board.
Motion agreed to and the House went into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: In this case the sum of $2,000 was voted and after the vote was exhausted the men were continued at work and further obligations incurred. What is the explanation of that?

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The engineer carried on the work up to a recent date because his opinion was that to leave the work as it was would lead to the danger of it being destroyed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: After the $2,000 had been exhausted and expenditure to the extent of $4,000 more incurred before it was voted, were the men paid their wages?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No, they were not paid and this vote is to pay them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Does the government owe $4,000 for wages and materials during September, October, November and December? Have the men been waiting all this time to get their pay?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: That is quite correct but the men understood that if they continued work they would have to wait until parliament made an appropriation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Does the minister commend such a practice as that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
I do not and I would not justify it except in the most exceptional case. In this case the engineer in charge reported to the chief engineer on January 6, 1909.
The landing pier under construction at St. Francois du Lac in Yamaska is in danger of being damaged during winter or spring freshets unless the work is continued and completed this winter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: When was the appropriation exhausted?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
Some time in the fall. He continues:
The urgent work yet to be done this winter is stone ballast, stringers, flooring, &c., requiring an additional use of $1,900, and for labour to complete the work, $2,300; total amount, $4,200. If work is continued persons working or supplying materials are willing to await payment until new appropriation is available.
The people understood that, but I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) that if possible this should never be done. In this case there were exceptional circumstances and the chief engineer allowed the resident engineer to proceed with the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: In case oi extreme urgency cannot the minister get an additional credit in a legal way?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: In cases of unforseen emergencies a Governor General's warrant could be obtained and probably this might come within that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the system of issuing Governor General's warrants is to meet cases of emergency _ and that the law contemplated, in sanctioning Governor General's warrants, that the system would remove all possible excuse for such an irregularity as this. If this were a case of real urgency why did not the minister asli for a Governor General's warrant? It is entirely infra dig, for Canada to ask people to work and wait for payment. We hear from all parts of the country that people have been asked to do work by the Dominion of Canada and its officials and then have not been paid. We had such a case in Lakevale, Nova Scotia, in which the workmen have not been paid and have been writing beseeching letters to the department and to their members for a considerable time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
In this particular case the chief engineer, perhaps because he was not fully impressed with the importance of it, did not call my attention to the matter until some time in February; he took the responsibility upon himself by reason of the peculiar circumstances of this case. I find that on the 15th of December he wrote to the resident engineer as follows:
Sir,-With regard to your stoppage of work at St. Francois du Lao and St. Michel, Yamaska, the department is informed that unless these works are continued and completed during this winter they are in danger of being damaged or carried away in the spring.
The appropriations for these works are, of course, exhausted, in fact are over expended, hut it is stated that labourers and parties supplying materials would be willing to await payment until the new appropriation required for completion is available.
Would you therefore give this matter your immediate attention and let me have a report stating whether it is urgent or not that these works should be continued until completed to prevent all chance of their being damaged, as above mentioned. You will also please let me know what amount is required to complete each of these works. As this is urgent, I would like to have a report without delay.
Mr. Belanger Teplied on the 6th of January by the letter I have quoted. In this particular case the explanation of the engineer is that the foreman allowed the work to go on for a short time after he had received notice not to exceed the appropriation, and then the chief engineer, having learned that it was necessary to proceed in order to prevent the works from being des-Mr. PUGSLEY.
troyed, wrote the resident engineer and received this reply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: When did he get the notice that the appropriation was exhausted?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I cannot tell exactly, but I presume some little time before December 15. My hon. friend speaks of this as if there were a number of cases. I venture to say my hon. friend has learned of every case there is. There have been only a very few cases, we do not allow this as a matter of practice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How many?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
Some two or three cases have come to my notice where there are comparatively small amounts, and two of these were cases in which the engineer had acted upon the printed estimates which were sent out and apparently the chief engineer had overlooked the making of a correction after the amount was reduced here in committee upon my motion. Those are two of the cases and this is the third case.
I do not know of any other case. We are very particular, I am particular in giving directions, and so is my chief engineer, that the resident engineers and the foremen all clearly understand what amount is available and that they must not exceed the appropriation. In this particular case there has been no hardship, because the men did this work which was apparently necessary in order to prevent the work that had been done from being destroyed, and it was clearly understood that they would have to wait for their pay until parliament made the appropriation. *

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
I do not think the minister quite understands the gravity of the matter which has been disclosed in this one instance accidentally. The minister says that this sort of thing has not occurred more than three times, so far as he knows. We have to take the minister's word that so far as it has come to him there have not been more than three cases, but I invite the attention of the minister to what is involved in this. There is no other way under which appropriations of money belonging to the treasury of Canada can be expended except either by vote of this House or by the authority of a Governor General's warrant. The Governor General's warrant is an expedient which the ministers on urgent occasion may avail themselves of while the House is not in session and where there is no appropriation, in order to complete or do some work which is unexpected, unforeseen and absolutely urgent. When once parliament, by its legislation, makes no provision for the unexpected, the unforeseen and the urgent, that is the course that must be pursued by the minister; he is sworn to take that course. In this case what happen-^-ed? Your vote was given, it was overexpended, your accommodating foreman did

not stop the men from working when he should have-and I would be glad if the minister would bring the exact date on which the foreman exceeded his instructions. The $2,000 was expended and a little more and then the minister, because he is responsible, drew a cheque on the treasury of the Dominion for $4,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No, my hon. friend is entirely wrong; that is just what we didn't do These men are not paid yet, and will never be paid unless this appropriation passes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I know exactly what I am saying, if the minister will allow me. I say the minister, having no vote, choosing not to go to council for a Governor General's warrant, drew a cheque on the treasury of the Dominion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: That is just what the minister did not do; no cheque was drawn for this sum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: If the minister will allow me I will show him what he has done. There is no means of getting this clearly into the head of the ministry unless you use language which is strong.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: But it is important it should be correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The minister drew a cheque on the treasury which he had no right to draw. He did not sign it on a piece of paper but he authorized his men to employ the workmen and promised them their pay. That is what I mean by saying that what he did was equivalent to drawing a cheque on the treasury of the Dominion, promising these men that at a certain date they would get their money. Had the minister any right to do that ? He acknowledges himself that he had not. My language was figurative.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Extremely figurative.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
I used it to make the minister understand the enormity of what he did. Would the minister, for instance, go into the bank and for a claim which was not due or for a work which was not authorized, authorize that bank to issue to him money payable on a certain date? Has he any right to do it? He knows he would not do it, he knows he could not rightfully do it and if he did attempt to do it, he would attempt to do what there was no law or reason for, and yet this is equivalent to that very same thing. My hon. friend behind me said that this was infra dig of the gov eminent. That is the smallest part of it, it is a system which is absolutely equivalent to drawing in advance from the treasury of the Dominion when you have no legal right or warrant. That is a very bad method of carrying on the business of the department. The minister gets out of these things easily. Yesterday we had a case in 103
which the minister and his predecessor expended $65,000 without any authority and against the express provision of the law by day's labour doing a work from year to year and never availing himself of the simple formality of going to the Governor in Council and getting an order in council to make his action legal. There is a statute specifying the course to be pursued by a minister in such a case and implicitly forbidding any other course. The minister has violated that statute over and over again. The St. John pipe line was not the first case in which it occurred, we had other cases a few days ago. How far are we going, how far is this parliament going to allow the minister to go in this arbitrary, illegal and unauthorized fashion? We pass a law in which we lay down the principle that these expenditures shall be made by tender and contract, but as a too rigid adherence to that principle would sometimes lead to trouble, we make an exception and provide that if. in the case of an expenditure up to $5,000, the minister has reason to believe the work could be better or moTe quickly done by day labour, he makes his request and gives his reasons to council, and if the council consents, the work is done in that way. But my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works and his predecessor have spent $65,000 upon that Carle-ton and Partridge island work and had the work done by day labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I thought we had passed that item.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I am using it as an illustration. I know that it bears heavily on the hon. minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: If he has a conscience which is not disturbed at all by such glaring violations of the law, and I take his word for it, I can understand how this does not affect him. But when there are violations after violations of the law, the question is whether parliament will give up its rights and leave such matters wholly to the discretion of an irresponsible minister. I do not think parliament wants to do that. It has few enough rights, and when it enacts a law, the minister should carry that law out; and a law regarding public expenditure is one of the most important we can pass. I place these matters before the minister as strongly as I can because they evidently do not disturb his conscience.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend took advantage of the right item on which to base his complaint. If he had condemned as forcibly yesterday the expenditure on the work at Partridge island as he has done t'o-day, his protest might have had some effect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I did deal with it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
But the item under consideration now is not such an item as affords my hon. friend reason to dwell upon it so forcibly, and for this reason. Parliament last session authorized this work to be proceeded with.
' Mr. FOSTER. Authorized the minister to do the work for $2,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
After expending $2,000, it was found that unless the work was continued and this additional money expended, what had been done would be in danger of being washed away. That was brought to the attention of my chief engineer and he brought it to my notice, and the resident engineer was authorized to go on with the work so far as was necessary to prevent its being destroyed during the coming spring. All the chief engineer did was to tell the resident engineer that the men who did this work and supplied the material had to take their chances of the money being voted by parliament. Let me call attention to what took place over and over again when my hon. friend was Minister of Finance, just as it is taking place to-day and has taken place under all administrations. Suppose a public building has to be erected, and is estimated to cost $100,000. Parliament usually votes one-third of the amount as being the sum which is likely to be spent during the coming year, and the contractor goes ahead. It is provided in the contract that if he goes beyond the amount appropriated by parliament, he must do so at his own risk. He is supposed to stop when that appropriation is exhausted. By the 1st of October the contractor has done work on the building to the value of one-third its estimated cost and the parliamentary appropriation is exhausted. Does he stop? Did he stop when my hon. friend was minister? No, he goes on with the work. He may do work to the extent of $75,000. In such a case what did my hon. friend do? He put in the supplementaries an amount sufficient to pay the contractor for all the work done during the current year exceeding the appropriation. He did that over and over again. What is the difference between such a case and the present instance? My hon. friends say that in the present instance, the putting in of the supplementary vote is equivalent to drawing a cheque on the treasury for $4,000. But when my hon. friend gave his contractor to understand that an amount would be put in the supplementaries to cover what he did during the current year in excess of the parliamentary appropriation, was he drawing a cheque on the treasury to that amount? If his contention be right, then every time you put an item in the supplementaries, you are drawing a cheque on the _ treasury, and pledging the public credit, and all these votes in the supple-Mr. FOSTER.
mentary estimates, amounting to $2,000,000 or $3,000,000, should not be there. Why are they there? They represent wages due, amounts due for rents and supplies, amounts due to contractors on public buildings and wharfs all over this country, and which were not wholly provided for in the main estimates of last year. That is why we ask to-day for these supplementary votes. My hon. friend may, with his keen intellect and his keen discernment of right and wrong, be able to see the distinction between the two cases, but I am not. No doubt it is the duty of the foreman to stop the work when he gets notice that the appropriation is exhausted, and his permitting it to go on can only be justified under very exceptional circumstances. In the opinion of the engineer, the case in question was one in which it was justifiable to go ahead and make the necessary expenditure to save the work from destruction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
The matter under discussion is one regarding which I have very particular knowledge. I know that all contractors are in the habit of doing work ahead of the appropriations. If the Department of Public Works or the Department of Railways and Canals, when they give out contracts, would notify the contractors that there was a certain amount to be appropriated and that after that appropriation was exhausted, the work for that year must stop, the contractors would tender on very different lines from those on which they do now. But under the late government, when my hon. friend from North Lanark was Minister of Railways, things were done in exactly the same way as at present. My hon. friend shakes his head, but I know they, were. If the contractors were told that after the appropriation was spent, they must cease their work, they would put in their tenders accordingly but the difficulty is that they put in their tenders expecting to go on and complete their work, after the appropriation is exhausted. They spend their money and they find they cannot get paid, and that is what causes the whole difficulty. T have called the attention of the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to this very matter. I believe the contractors who have spent their money under those conditions, should be paid interest, because they have to pay interest to the bank'- which are carrying them. I think it only fair that a contractor should be paid interest on the money due him from the date it is due until the date it is paid. If the department would notify them that they must work under certain conditions, then the contractors would put in higher prices, but they are not notified. I know sufficient about the whole situation to know that the proper thing to do is for the two

large spending departments of Public Works and Railways to inform the contractors that there's a certain amount to be expended, and when that is Bpent, they must stop the work. Or else tell them: Complete your work, and if we have not the money, we will pay interest on what you expend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Let me show the distinction between the instance given by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) and the present instance. I will explain how we did it when we were running the government. Suppose we had a contract on the Canadian Pacific Railway the estimated expenditure on which was $5,000,000, but the amount to be expended during the year was $500,000, and that amount was asked for and voted. We entered into a contract for the $5,000,000, or for the $500,000, as the case might be. But the contractor knew, as every contractor for the government knows, that the only amount available during the year was the appropriation of parliament. He was notified when the appropriation ran out. But he relied upon the government to have a sum voted next year to carry on the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: When he was in office did not he have supplementary estimates for the current year?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: For what purpose?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: For the purpose of covering the work, just as the hon. gentle-(Mr. Pugsley) has done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Just so,-where parliament had not already supplied it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: But, look at the difference between the two cases. Here is a vote for $2,000 to complete a work

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No, the hon. member is entirely in error; it was towards the work, not to complete it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Was there any intimation that more would be required?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It must have been the full amount.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No. no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
If it was a work estimated to cost over $5,000, the minister had no right to do it by day's labour, but ought to have given it out by tender and contract. He did not do this. Why? For the simple reason that he thought $2,000 would complete the work. The House votes $2,000, and the minister goes on by day's 103i
work. After the appropriation runs out, the engineer, who is the judge of the emergency of this case, orders the work continued, and tells the men that they will be paid. So, the cases are entirely different. A contractor may have a contract for $5,000,000, the year's appropriation towards which may be only $150,000. If the contractor does $200,000 worth of work, it is quite legitimate to ask for $50,000 in the supplementary estimates to make up the difference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me to ask him this question?: Does not that show that the minister approved of the contractor doing work to the extent of $50,000 beyond the amount voted?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I am sure the minister understands the distinction. This work was to be completed for $2,000

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The fact that the minister violated the law in going on by day's labour, if the estimated cost was $6,000, shows that he did not expect to spend that amount. If it were a work of emergency, the minister's duty, when the $2,000 appropriation was expended, was to have an order in council passed in favour of going on with the work as an emergency work. But look at the position in which the great Dominion of Canada is placed- owing its men for days' wages for six or seven months, awaiting supplementary estimates in order to get the money to pay them. There is a silent contract between the minister and these men that they are simply to be allowed to go on with the work and will wait for their pay until the minister gets a supplementary estimate. That is not an enviable position in which to place the country, and, if I understand him aright, the minister knows it. He tries to excuse it all, but in a very lame fashion, -it is wrong to do it, and hopes that the same thing will not occur again.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
As the minister does not seem to understand it yet, I would like to add a word. The minister takes as one example a large contract. Let us take a concrete case :	We will say work going
on for dredging in the city and harbour of St. John. The estimates are laid on the table and when they come up in committee the minister is asked how much it will take to complete the work, and he gives the estimate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Suppose that the minister is not asked, and makes no statement?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I can hardly conceive

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
Does not the hon. member know that these Quebec items went

through and no one asked a single question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: But it is not the duty of the minister to slip through votes, even in hurried moments, without giving to the House at least the elementary information with regard to them. And if the minister had a vote for $2,000 for work which he knew could not be completed for that amount, he was not treating the House fairly if he did not tell the House, in all frankness, that it would cost more to complete the work. The minister's duty is clear, and I am sure no one sees it more clearly than he does. Here is a public work, the quantities and estimated cost of which are known. An appropriation is made for it. The minister makes a contract for the construction, which contract binds him to pay for the work so much on progress estimates as the work is done. Nobody can tell just how much will be done in one year. It will depend very much upon the circumstances that meet the contractor as he proceeds. But the contract is plain, if the contractor finishes that work he is to receive so much money. The contract is plain, because parliament has agreed to the expenditure of that large amount of money for that work, and it proposes to pay for it, and authorizes its minister to enter into a contract to get the work done. This case is entirely different. Here is a piece of work which is done by day's labour. The minister does not tell the House when he brings down his estimates and gets his $2,000, that it is to cost more. If he had told the House that it was to cost $6,000, he would then have been obliged to let it by tender and contract, or to have got the authority of council in order to allow the work to be done by day's work. But he did not tell the House that, it is $2,000, and that is all the minister has, and it is all he has a right to pledge. The cases are as different as they can be, and the minister sees it as clearly as any man in this House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
I wish I had the ability of my hon. friend to make black appear white and white appear black, but I am not able to do that. If I understand my hon. _ friend, this would have been all right if, at the last session of parliament when I asked for the $2,000, I had stated that the work was likely to cost some $10,080; and then, if I had entered into a contract to have the work done, and the contractor had gone on and finished the work just as it is now being done, in that case I would have been quite right in coming to parliament and saying: Although I have only $2,000 of an appropriation, yet I have given the contract for $10,000, the contractor has gone on faster than we anticipated, he has finished up his work, and I must ask parliament for a vote of an ad-Mr. PUGSLEY.
ditional $4,000, or all that is required, to pay him. That would have been all right, according to my hon. friend, would it not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Go on and make your argument.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend would not agree to that. The only difference is that here the country has got good value. These poor labouring men have gone ahead and have done this work under the direction of the engineer, done work which was absolutely necessary in order to save horn destruction what they had already done, and for which they were paid out of the $2,000, and now we are asking parliament to give us the money to pay these men for their labour, and pay for the materials which have been put into the work. I can see a technical difference between the two.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Can you not see a legal difference?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
No, I am not able to see a legal difference, because in the case of a contractor he has to go on and take the risk of parliament voting his money. The contractor had no business legally to spend one dollar under his contract beyond the appropriation of parliament. What does the contractor do? The contract expressly provides that the minister is not bound to make a payment until and unless parliament makes a further appropriation. If parliament does not make the appropriation, the minister is under no obligation and the government is under no obligation. The contractor could not go into the Exchequer Court and recover a single dollar. It is entirely a voluntary matter on the part of parliament to vote in the supplementary estimates the requisite amount to cover the over-expenditure which the contractor has made during the current year. While I say this, I am also free to say that this is something which the engineer should not permit except under the most exceptional circumstances. I do not attempt to justify it as a practice which ought to be generally pursued. The engineer thought in this case that he was doing what was. in the public interest, he thought the work he was doing was necessary to save from destruction that which had been already done. He fully explained to these men that they would have to wait, he explained that they could not expect the money until parliament voted it. As I understand it, the distinction is merely a technical one. In each case the work has been done; in the one case the contractor, and in the other case the men, simply look to parliament to do what it is not bound to do. and it is for this committee now to consider whether this work having been done, it being a useful public work, and having been done in the public interest, it should provide money for

the purpose of paying these men for their labour and to pay for the material.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: My hon. friend is an eminent lawyer, stands high in his profession; I am not a lawyer, but I am willing to put my common sense against the minister's law, and submit it to this committee. The minister came down to parliament, he proposed this work, he told parliament it would cost $10,000. Parliament gave an appropriation of $2,000 towards the completion of that work. That authorized the minister to enter into a contract for the work, he called for tenders and let the contract. With that authorization he entered into a contract with a man to perform that work, and upon the work being properly performed and certified to, that man would have a claim for $10,000. That is the one case fair and square.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Would he have a claim until parliament voted the money ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It makes no difference. The very moment you make a contract with a man by which he is to carry out that work, he is to receive on the completion of that work, $10,000. That is a hard and fast contract. My hon. friend said that if he went on and built it, it was a mere matter of grace, or favour, or good will for parliament to make an appropriation to pay him. Now I will put my common sense against his law, and I will say this: If the minister entered in that way into a contract with a man to perform a work upon the completion of which he should be paid by this country $10,000, if the man went on and performed the work, advanced his own money when the appropriation was run out, paid his own men, bought his own material and performed the work himself, and said, there is your work, put on your inspector, and the inspector goes on and says it is all right, that man can collect from this country his $10,000, unless the country is mean enough not to give him the fiat to go to court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: My hon. friend omitted to state that in all these contracts it is expressly provided that if the contractor goes beyond the appropriation he does it at his own risk.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
Exactly, he does so at his own risk, and he pays his men, if he wanted to pay before the six months are over. You are not then in the deplorable condition of having John Smith, and Tom Brown, and a dozen others owed by the government six months for work, and the government not able to pay them, and this country held up in that sort of fashion. He can go on and say, ' I will complete this work, I have got the men and material here, I will provide my own money and complete it, and when it. is completed I will get my money from the government.'
There is no government in the world that could withhold that money from him. He takes his own risk, but the risk amounts to nothing. This is the difference. The minister in this case came for a $2,000 expenditure, if he had come for a $6,000 expenditure, he would have had to let it by tender and contract. He dit not do it, and he came for his $2,000 and got it, that is all he should have expended. His engineer did wrong, and he himself did wrong, in allowing his engineer to enter into any kind of an understanding with these men to go on and complete this work for $4,000 more, and promising that in four or five, or six months afterward this parliament would pay it. But there is no use in my hon. friend and myself showing our comparative excellence in law over these items, so I think we will stop.
Batiscan-dredging channel at month of river, $4,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This is under contract to Randolph Macdonald, and' is to finish up the payments to him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How much has it cost?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It has cost somewhere in the vicinity of $70,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What is being done?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This is for dredging at the mouth of the channel and improving the navigable river to a depth of six feet at low water, a distance of five miles up the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
What is the business on
the Batiscan river?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: There is considerable local traffic. Market boats call there. The Richelieu & Ontario Navigation Company's boats call, and it is a great convenience to farmers to have steamers come in and give them a cheap means of getting their produce to market. The mail boats call there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The Batiscan flows into what river?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Into the St. Lawrence. It is 21 miles below Three Rivers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What point are you dredging up to?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Ste. Genevieve, five miles from the mouth.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What is the population of Ste. Genevieve?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: 3,000, including the parish and town.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: If you take in a whole county you can easily get 3,000 and more. You might go right up to the height of land.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The census will show you that my statement is correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This work is being done at the very reasonable charge of 17 cents per cubic yard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: If, in our time, we had undertaken to spend $70,000 in every little village and in every little river I think there would have been ructions in this parliament and in the country as well. Seventy thousand dollars is a tremendous amount of money to spend. What is the commercial equivalent that is to come from the expenditure of $70,000?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: First of all I want to correct a statement I made as to the contractor. It is not Mr. Randolph Macdonald, bult the contractors are Messrs. Du-fresne, Turcotte & Marchildon. My hon. friend says there would have been ructions. When-years ago?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes, at any time when we had good sentiment in the House and in the country..

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: There -was not as much revenue as we have now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: And there was not as much call for revenue.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: That is probably because the country has about doubled in growth and importance and everything that contributes to the development of the nation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: There were not as many taxes then as now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: And not as much ability to pay them as now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I do not know about that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I think we had better discuss the item.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Well, go on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Besides the town of Ste. Genevieve there are on the river, Batiscan, St. Prospere, St. Stanislas and St. Narcisse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Are these places below Ste. Genevieve?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: They are all accommodated by this steamship service.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Is that so? The minister says they will be; will they be?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
That is my information. Apparently there was a petition presented in favour of this work. I have not the petition with me now because this was entered upon some few years ago, but the people of Batiscan, St. Prospere, St. Stanislas and St. Narcisse represented that it would be a great advantage to them to have steamers calling and to be thus enabled to send their products by water, it being much cheaper than by railway. I think we ought not to take too strpng a Mr. LAVERGNE.
stand against improving the waterways of the country. A reasonable expenditure in dredging out these rivers to enable the steamers to get to the various settlements of the country to enable the people to get their produce to market by water is a matter of a good deal of importance. Water transportation is very cheap as compared with railway transportation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I do not know about it being any cheaper when you have to do it at a cost of $70,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It is cheaper for the people and while the initial cost may be larger when it is once done it is done for all time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What amount was voted last year for this work ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: There was an appropriation of $15,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Was it all expended ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: And how much more ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It takes $4,000 to finish the expenditure of the current year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: They spent everything last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This $66,000 has been running for a number of years. All we spent last year was $18,867 and we had $15,000 of an appropriation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What will it cost to finish it up to the railway bridge ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I have not the memorandum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What depth of water will it give ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Six feet at low tide.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Do the Richelieu steamers run up there ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Flat bottom boats ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: A number of boats of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company; I do not say their biggest boats.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Will the minister explain how the Richelieu steamers are going to get up with six feet of water ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Their big steamers do not go there, but they have a boat which makes close connection with the mail steamers on the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Oh, I was buoying myself up with the idea that these magnificent steamers went up there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The mail steamers do not go up the different rivers, I think the mail steamers connect with the boat which runs up the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Perhaps it is a row boat.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: We would like to know what it will cost.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It all depends on how much dredging we will do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This is in the county of Champlain. I am sorry the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin) is not here because I know he would defend the work if he were present. There are large saw-mills located upon the river and boats go into the river to get lumber.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Saw-mills at Ste. Genevieve?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
Yes there is one at Ste. Genevieve and one at the mouth of the river Batiscan.
Riviere Bonaventure-training pier, $4,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This is to make payment on a contract for work done during the year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: We have already made our protest against that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What is the meaning of a * training ' pier ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It is to train the current so that it scours out the channel and directs the flow of the silt.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Does it prove itself fairly amenable to training?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It does as a rule.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I thought that a current was rather obstinate, uncertain and difficult to train ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No, it is wonderful how you can direct it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How much will it take to put this current into a good condition of training ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How much has been expended altogether ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
It will "be about $27,-
000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: When that amount is spent what will the minister have ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: We will have a training pier 1,200 feet long, 22 feet wide on top, 14 feet high at the outer end and 5 feet above high water spring tides.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The design is to keep the current out of the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It is rather to concentrate the current into a narrower channel so that it will carry away the silt.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: And allow of better navigation ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What is the size of the city to which the navigation goes ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It is one of the largest shipping points upon all that coast.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Does the lumber go out by water ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Is the minister sure of that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Is the lumber loaded on this pier?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I do not know but I should think not.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: May I be allowed to say that the Bonaventure river is the largest river in the county of Bonaventure and probably the largest in the Gaspesian peninsula.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What does that mean?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
It is the outlet for the famous Robitaille timber limits which are known as the best timber limits in the province of Quebec. They were held by the late Lieutenant-Governor Robitaille and his family for 25 years and three years ago they were purchased by a syndicate headed by Senator Edwards of Ottawa, called the Cascapedia Trading Lumber Company. It was said at the time that $400,000 was paid for the limits which are now worked by this Canadian Company which has an agency in Buffalo. There is a large mill situated at the mouth of the river which formerly belonged to Mr. LeBlanc and which was purchased by this company. There are men living in Bonaventure county to-day who remember that 40 years ago three masted schooners used to enter the Bonaventure river and proceed to the basin in rear of the barrachois where there is a depth of 25 feet of water. When there limits commenced to be worked logs and stumps floated down the river and becoming embedded in the sand'they completely blocked up the channel. The parish of Bonaventure River, has a population of about 1,800 and is about the largest parish in the county. This lumber company has gone very extensively into the operation of these mills and means have to be found to enable them to carry on their business. I think there was a statement made to the department last year showing that from 60 to 75 steamers and sailing craft of all kinds had been loaded with lumber and railway ties at that point. ^ Mr. Crocket, my former opponent, who is the largest dealer in railway ties in the province of

Quebec, sent several hundred thousand from that point. These ties came down the Bonaventure river and were shipped to different parts of the United States, and even to Mexico and South America. These steamers and sailing vessels which took this freight had to anchor a mile or a mile and a half out in the open without any shelter from storms. The lumber and the ties had to be conveyed in scows and some of these were lost last year with their cargoes, and the lives of the crews endangered. Mr. LeBlanc, who was a large lumber operator there, made several requests on the government for facilities to carry on his industry. Mr. Breen, who was engineer of the district for twenty-five years, and who is still the engineer in charge of the district of Quebec, sent in one or two interesting reports showing that it was out of the question to build a wharf at Bonaventure river because it is flat land extending out into the bay, and the only way in which assistance could be given was to build a training pier which would serve to scour the channel of the river. This pier has been built at a cost of $27,000, and the idea is to dredge out the channel, the training pier being intended to prevent the south and west winds from filling up the river with sand and other accumulations. When some dredging is done, the vessels which now have to lie out in the bay will be able to enter the basin and load there under all conditions of weather. Anyone who has visited the locality will admit that this is a very useful work. The village of Bonaventure River itself is growing very rapidly. The Cascapedia Lumber Company has erected a large departmental store which is a new feature in the Gaspe country, and I think they employ 400 men during this winter. More lumbering is done at that one point than probably at any other point on the Gaspe peninsula.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Are there mills there?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Yes. Mr. LeBlanc's mill was purchased by the Edwards syndicate and it employs 150 men. It is a sawmill with all modern appliances and has been working day-and night. It is one of the attractions of the place to see it. The Bonaventure river has three mouths emptying into the Baie des Chaleurs, and it runs for 60 or 70 miles into the Gaspe peninsula. There is a peculiarity caused by the development of the lumber operations in that, while in all the rest of that country the settlements are on the front, there is on the Bonaventure river the parish of St. Alphonse de Caplan located some distance from the bay. I think there are settlements now up to the 12th range from the Baie des Chaleurs into the back country as a consequence of these lumbering operations.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The river itself is not navigable, I suppose?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Not navigable. The fishermen go there, the salmon fishermen; it is navigable for that purpose.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: And do they still load outside?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: They have to load out in the open, perhaps a mile and a-half out. Mr. Leblanc, the manager of the firm, informed me last year that the vessels have to anchor a mile or a mile and a-half out and the lumber is taken out to them in scows. Sometimes a change in the wind over night will delay operations or toss a scow over. They have no protection from the south and west, although they have protection from the east.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The training pier, costing $27,000, has not benefited them so as to allow them to bring the vessels up and load inside.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The last report of the resident engineer is that the pier does not go far enough, it will have to go 150 feet further to reach the low water mark.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Is it proposed to do that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: An application has been made, but it has not been granted yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It is no good.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Please do not tell Mr. Speaker it is no good, he has been urging an extension of the pier, but it has not been agreed on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Dredging will have to be done to give a proper channel to the mouth of the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Is there not a wide mud flat for a mile or so out from the Bonaventure river?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The bay all over is very shallow.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The vessel could not get within a mile or a mile and a-half of the river?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I could not say that it is a mile; I am not a judge of distances on the water, but it is a long distance out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The pier would not be of use until a mile of dredging is done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Dredging would have to be done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: *1 can see where several millions could be spent before you can get a three-masted schooner to the mouth of the Bonaventure river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I do not think so; my hon. friend frequently visits the Gaspe peninsula, he is a sportsman-

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I suppose he goes fishing there when he is not photographing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
We have the finest salmon fishing in the world there. A large amount of business is done at the Bona-venture river and it is only fair that some assistance should be given to it.
_ Mr. AMES. If there is a chance of making a protected harbour and getting the requisite depth with a reasonable expense, it might properly be made, but as I understand, this river, like the little Pasbebiac, spreads out as soon as it reaches tide water and makes a wide mud flat. If this training pier is only a preliminary which must be followed by dredging operations, to form a channel for three-quarters of a mile or a mile from the mouth of the river out to deep water, it would seem that we are making a useless expenditure now or else this expense can only be made useful by an additional expenditure of many hundreds of thousands.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: We have secured some valuable information and it whets our appetite for more. We find, in the first place, that a training pier 1,200 feet in length, and costing $27,000, has already been built, and, in the second place, that the training pier has actually proved of no benefit at all to navigation, and the representative of the county says that the pier will never prove of any benefit to navigation unless it is made longer, at an added expense. How much longer must it be?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
150 feet.
Mr. FOSTkER. 150 feet has to be added before it will have a chance to be of any service towards deepening the channel. Even then it will be of no advantage until you dredge out a mud flat for a mile or a mile and a-half.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Sailing vessels always stay out a long distance in case of squalls.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: So we will have to lengthen the pier and then dredge out this mud flat forming a channel which, in a river like that, with its silt is likely to fill up within a year. $70,000 has already been spent in getting a six-foot channel at Batiscan for less, than three miles. For the ocean vessels that will come here you must have a depth of much more than six feet, I suppose from 20 to 30 feet, and I would like to know what the estimate of the amount of dredging required here is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: My hon. friend is greatly exaggerating and magnifying the probable cost even of doing the dredging.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I have not named a sum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The report is that there will be 23,000 yards of dredging, mostly sand and mud. The Batiscan dredging cost 17 cents, and if you put this at 25 cents the cost would be only $5,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What depth will that give?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Eight feet at low tide. The tide rises 8 feet so that will be 16 feet but when you get into the inner harbour or basin there will be 20 feet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: But you have to get in there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: You can get in at high tide. My hon. friend knows that in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick there are many places which are dry at low tide, where a large lumber shipping business has been carried on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The channel is the vital thing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The vessels would go in and out at high tide. Many quite large vessels do not draw over 16 feet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How much do the vessels draw that do load there?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Those that lay out in the St. Lawrence would draw more, but those that go into the inner harbour would be adapted for that trade.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Tranship outside?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: This is to provide for transhipment. Consequently you must have ocean vessels coming up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Many do not draw over 16 feet, and the larger number of vessels carrying lumber do not draw over 14 feet. Sailing vessels only draw 14 feet and many only 12, which take away very large cargoes of lumber.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Are these steamers to which the minister refers?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Some are steamers. Two years ago, Messrs. Thos Crocket & Co., a well known lumbering firm, loaded the largest steamer that ever left the province of Quebec with railway ties for Mexico. It was a record shipment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How much would that vessel draw?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: From 16 to 18 feet. The town of Campbellton is at the head of the bay and the most prosperous town on the northern shore of New Brunswick, and the steamers which go there now cannot take on full cargoes. They take until they draw about 12 feet of water and then drop down the river and finish there. If steamers could go into the natural basin and take on one-half or three-quarters of their cargo, the remainder could be taken on further down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
I have no objection to doing anything reasonable for the country-

side, because the country districts have claims as well as the cities, but when we boil this down, we find that the $27,000 which has been spent and the balance that will be spent is all absolutely for the advantage of a rich syndicate which has very valuable limits and which is working these limits for its own profit. It would have been a small thing for a rich syndicate, in which Senator Edwards is represented, to have done something themselves towards this expenditure instead of loading it on to the country. All the more so because the Dominion government gets no revenue at all from it. The work no doubt helps the parish and the parish above, but it is very doubtful whether we should unduly load the revenues of this country in our hurry to do a work which a large and rich lumber company should do for themselves.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: I am very glad to learn that the lumber trade have enlisted the sympathies of the Minister of Public Works, and I presume this expenditure is intended to compensate that trade somewhat for the competition they have to meet through the free admission of American lumber. But I have been endeavouring, ever since I came here, to ascertain what is the policy of the government with regard to where they should place these wharfs and where they should not build them. I am led to believe from the discussion this afternoon that this $27,000 has been expended at this place because a lumber company, which bought the limits for about $400,000 and employs some 400 men, and a village of 1,800 population and a parish with a total population of some 3,000 are benefited by it. I would remind the Minister of Public Works that last year there was an appropriation of $2,000 for a wharf at a place somewhat similar but that wharf has never been gone on with. And at that particular point, limits were purchased by a company to the value of over a million dollars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What place is that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: It is a small place called Cache Bay on Lake Nipissing. This $2,000 was in the estimates last year but does not appear there this year. The limits purchased at that place are three or four times the value of those in connection with the particular item under discussion, and the men employed are three times more numerous than in this case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: That was in Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What I would like to find out is on what basis the government decides these things. In business tne test would be what we were going to get back in dollars and cents and what business was going on in the locality. If the government had any such policy, I would

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: like to know why that particular vote of $2,000 is not in the estimates this year ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The work at Cache bay stands over, as do a great many others, in pursuance of the policy of retrenchment during the coming year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: They voted wrong the last election.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext:
That cannot be the reason because I have kept in a large vote for a dam at Latchford which is in that constituency. But this particular work did not seem urgent, and we thought it might stand over.
Rivihre du Loup (en haut)-dredging and other improvements at mouth, $6,100.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Who has the contract ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: Poupore and Company. It was given after public advertisement and tender.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: What amount will complete ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: The expenditure was $31,219, and the appropriation $25,200. This is to pay the balance. This will not complete. It depends on how far along we may go. We have got to make a complete survey before we can tell the total cost of the work that may be required.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY FREIGHT CLERKS, HALIFAX AND ST. JOHN.
speechtext: How much has been spent so far altogether ?
